title: Recursive CTEs: Base Plus Step
objective: After this lesson you will be able to write WITH RECURSIVE queries (anchor + recursive step + termination), walk hierarchies and generate sequences in pure SQL, and prove termination before running.
why: Intermediate Ch.2 teased it: a CTE that references itself. Org charts, prerequisite chains, category trees, dependency graphs — any data that points at itself — plus sequence generation (date series, number ranges for gap analysis). Recursion turns SQL from a row-filtering language into one that walks structures, and it is the single most interview-distinguishing SQL skill.

blocks.text: A recursive CTE has three parts: the **anchor** (starting rows), **`UNION ALL`** (almost always ALL — UNION's dedup can break iteration), and the **recursive step** (joins the CTE to produce the next layer). The engine repeats the step on new rows until it produces nothing. Termination is your responsibility: every recursion needs a condition that eventually yields zero rows.

blocks.code:
-- Count 1..10 in pure SQL: anchor, step, and the stop condition
WITH RECURSIVE counter(n) AS (
  SELECT 1            -- anchor: where the walk starts
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM counter WHERE n < 10  -- step + stop in one line
)
SELECT n FROM counter;
blocks.caption: The minimal recursion: without WHERE n < 10 it never terminates

blocks.text: Read the execution as waves: wave 0 is {1}; the step maps each wave to the next ({2}, {3}, …); the WHERE filters wave 11 to empty, and iteration stops. The stop condition lives *inside* the recursive step — forget it and the query runs until the engine's iteration limit kills it (SQLite: SQLITE_LIMIT_CTE_RECURSION; PostgreSQL: statement timeout territory).

blocks.title: Prove termination on paper first
blocks.text: Before running any recursion, point at the condition that shrinks the frontier: a counter with an upper bound, a depth limit, or a visited-set that grows. Cycles in the data (A→B→A) defeat naive walks — carry a path/depth guard. Infinite recursion is the one SQL mistake that punishes with hangs, not errors.

Hierarchies store parent pointers (`manager_id`, `parent_id`); recursion walks them. Track **depth** as you go (anchor depth 0, step depth+1) and build a **path** string for readable lineage. The pattern below uses an inline org table — in production it joins your real employees/categories table.

blocks.code:
-- Org walk: depth + path carried through the recursion (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
WITH RECURSIVE org(id, name, mgr) AS (
  VALUES (1, 'Ava', NULL), (2, 'Ben', 1), (3, 'Cy', 1), (4, 'Dee', 2)
),
chain(id, name, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0, name FROM org WHERE mgr IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT o.id, o.name, c.depth + 1, c.path || ' > ' || o.name
  FROM org o JOIN chain c ON o.mgr = c.id
  WHERE c.depth < 20
)
SELECT name, depth, path FROM chain ORDER BY path;
blocks.caption: Depth and path as carried state — the hierarchy walk template

blocks.text: Three reusable mechanics: the anchor selects roots (`mgr IS NULL`); the step joins children to the accumulated chain (not to the base table's roots); carried columns (`depth`, `path`) accumulate context the final SELECT presents. `WHERE c.depth < 20` is the seatbelt — even clean hierarchies deserve one against corrupt cycles.

Recursion also *generates* rows: number ranges, date series. The killer app is **gap analysis** — generate the complete expected set, LEFT JOIN actuals, keep the NULLs (Intermediate absence dialect). 'Which course ids have no enrollments in a range?' and 'which dates had zero signups?' are sequence-minus-reality queries.

blocks.code:
-- Gap hunt template: expected series LEFT JOIN reality (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
WITH RECURSIVE series(n) AS (
  SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM series WHERE n < 16
)
SELECT s.n AS course_id
FROM series s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = s.n
WHERE e.id IS NULL;
blocks.caption: Generate the expected, subtract the actual — absence via recursion

blocks.title: Sandbox note
blocks.text: Recursion needs WITH RECURSIVE, which the flat-SELECT sandbox doesn't execute — all recursion runs in real SQLite/PostgreSQL. Sandbox practice below verifies the *anchor-shaped* flat pieces (roots, children-of-X) that your recursive steps are built from.

blocks.query: SELECT DISTINCT course_id FROM enrollments ORDER BY course_id;
blocks.note: Run this reality inventory in the sandbox — which ids actually occur. The gap template subtracts exactly this set from the generated series: in a real database the series comes from WITH RECURSIVE, the reality from this same flat shape.

items: Recursion = anchor + UNION ALL + self-referencing step + in-step stop condition
UNION ALL (not UNION) for iteration; dedup can corrupt wave semantics
Carry depth and path as state; seatbelt every walk against cycles
Generate-then-subtract (series LEFT JOIN reality) finds gaps in sequences, dates, ids
Prove termination on paper: the frontier must shrink to empty

exercise.prompt: Build a prerequisite chain walk. Assume a table prereq(course_id, needs_id) with rows (8,5),(5,3),(3,1) meaning '8 needs 5 needs 3 needs 1'. (a) In the sandbox, practice the seed-then-expand mechanics on real tables: first the anchor-shaped query (developer's direct enrollments), then the one-hop expansion (their course titles) — two flat queries. (b) For real SQLite/PostgreSQL, write the WITH RECURSIVE walk from course 8 collecting the full chain with depth, terminating safely.
hints: Anchor: the direct prerequisite of 8 (needs_id of the row with course_id = 8), depth 1. Model prereq as a VALUES CTE or a real table — same shape.
Step: join prereq ON prereq.course_id = chain.current_id, collecting needs_id with depth + 1. Stop: no row has course_id = 1, so the walk ends naturally — plus an explicit depth guard.
Expected chain: 5 (d1), 3 (d2), 1 (d3). If your walk returns duplicates, check UNION ALL vs UNION and the join direction.
exercise.solution:
-- (b) real SQLite / PostgreSQL
WITH RECURSIVE prereq(course_id, needs_id) AS (
  VALUES (8, 5), (5, 3), (3, 1)
),
chain(current_id, depth) AS (
  SELECT needs_id, 1 FROM prereq WHERE course_id = 8
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.needs_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM prereq p JOIN chain c ON p.course_id = c.current_id
  WHERE c.depth < 20
)
SELECT current_id AS prerequisite, depth FROM chain ORDER BY depth;
-- 5/d1, 3/d2, 1/d3: then nothing needs course 1, walk ends.
exercise.why: The walk mirrors graph traversal: anchor seeds the frontier, the step expands it, exhaustion terminates it. VALUES-as-table keeps the exercise self-contained; production swaps in the real table with zero shape change — which is why the template transfers directly.

quiz.q: What are the three mandatory parts of a recursive CTE?
options: Anchor (seed rows), UNION ALL, self-referencing step with a stop condition
quiz.explain: Waves need a start (anchor), a wave function (recursive step over UNION ALL), and exhaustion (stop condition yielding zero rows). Missing any one: no start, corrupted iteration, or a hang.

quiz.q: Why UNION ALL rather than UNION in the recursive step?
options: UNION's dedup can remove rows the iteration still needs and corrupt wave semantics; ALL preserves every generated row
quiz.explain: Iteration correctness depends on complete waves. Dedup between waves can swallow frontier rows (and legitimately repeated values), breaking counts and termination. ALL is the correct default.

quiz.q: A hierarchy walk hangs on production data but worked in testing. Most likely cause and guard?
options: A cycle in the data (A→B→A) defeats naive termination — carry depth/path with an explicit bound
quiz.explain: Testing used a clean tree; production has a cycle, so the frontier never empties. Depth/path guards bound every walk regardless of data hygiene — seatbelts, not optimism.

quiz.q: How do you find 'dates with zero signups' using recursion?
options: Generate the full date series recursively, LEFT JOIN signups, keep NULLs — expected minus actual
quiz.explain: Absence needs a universe to subtract from. Recursion generates the expected set; the anti-join reveals gaps. Same template serves id ranges and sequence holes.

summary: Recursion walks what joins can't reach: anchor seeds, UNION ALL steps expand, stop conditions (plus seatbelts) terminate. Carry depth and path, generate-then-subtract for gaps, and never run an unproven walk on production data.
next: You can walk trees — but analytics mostly ranks peers, not ancestors. Next: window functions primer (ranks, partitions, frames), with full depth reserved for the dedicated course.
